chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Azdi, from one of our companions, raising it (to the Imam), said:

A man complained to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), saying, 'I am a complaining man.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Where is it from the Blessed?' I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you, and what is the Blessed?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'The sugar.' I said, 'Which sugar, may I be sacrificed for you?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Your Suleymaniyya, this.'

key_terms.الْمُبَارَكُ: The Blessed (one who is blessed or brings blessing)
key_terms.سُلَيْمَانِيُّكُمْ: Your Suleymaniyya (a specific variety of sugar from the region)

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) identify as the 'Blessed' remedy for complaints?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) identifies sugar as the 'Mubarak' (blessed) remedy, specifically highlighting the 'Suleymaniyya' variety, which reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the medicinal and spiritual purity of natural substances. This narration underscores the tradition of using food as medicine, linking physical well-being with divine blessing (barakah), a concept deeply rooted in both Quranic teachings and Prophetic practice within Shia jurisprudence.
